newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Evacuees leave Albania, West pins hopes on OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Evacuees leave Albania, West pins hopes on OSCE.

text.p: European special envoy Franz Vranitzky held crisis talks with Albanian government leaders aboard an Italian warship on Friday as Western nations deployed helicopters and ships to rescue their nationals from chaotic Albania.

While Europe and the United States pinned their hopes on Vranitzky's mission making some progress towards ending the growing chaos in the Balkan state, their governments pressed ahead with evacuating thousands of foreign nationals, fearing bloodshed in the streets of Tirana.
The European Union said it was working closely with the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and NATO to coordinate an urgent response to the Albanian crisis.

"The Union is coordinating closely with the OSCE and will liaise actively with NATO and other organisations, so that appropriate action can be taken urgently," the EU said in a statement released in The Hague by the Dutch presidency.
"The European Union expresses grave concern at the breakdown of civil order in Albania."
British officials said the OSCE would meet in emergency session in Vienna on Saturday to discuss the Albania crisis.

The United States sent in Sea Knight and Sea Stallion helicopters, with Cobras providing protection, into a central Tirana football stadium and evacuees were expected to be flown to U.S. battleships in the Adriatic.
Around 100 Italians and other nationals were plucked out of Tirana in an early morning operation by Italian military helicopters on Friday.
Italy's defence ministry said an Italian military AB-212 helicopter was pierced by two bullets while it was acting as an armed escort for other helicopters in the evaucation mission in Tirana.
The Foreign Office in London said 131 British and other foreign nationals had left the port of Durres and were on their way to Brindisi in Italy.
French helicopters were reported to be ready to evacuate around 70 of its nationals who were travelling from Tirana to Durres.
In Geneva, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) urged Italy and Greece to allow Albanians fleeing the violence to enter and stay "as long as necessary."
The U.N. was helping the governments of both countries to prepare for a "possible influx," though no mass movement has been detected, UNHCR spokesman Kris Janowski said.

An uneasy calm returned to the streets of Tirana after more than 24 hours of wild shooting. Tanks appeared on the streets on Thursday night, patrolling a central boulevard near the presidency and other government buildings.

Italy, bracing for a flood of refugees escaping Albania across the Adriatic Sea, was playing a pivotal role in organising talks between the OSCE, the Albanian government and rebel leaders in the south of the country.

Italian helicopters transported Vranitzky and his 10-member delegation to the Italian frigate Aliseo in the Adriatic at around 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) where they held immediate talks with Albania's newly-installed Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, Foreign Minister Arjan Starova and army chief of staff General Adem Copani.
An OSCE spokeswoman told Reuters in Vienna by telephone from the ship that rebel leaders from towns in southern Albania were expected to join at around 2 p.m. (1300 GMT).
"We are not sure if the members of the Albanian government will stay and meet with them but that is what we hope," the spokeswoman added.

Representatives of the National Committee of Public Salvation, an umbrella grouping of rebel towns in southern Albania, were holding a meeting in the Albanian port town of Vlore, where Italian helicopters were due to pick them up to transport them to the Aliseo.

Hundreds of thousands of people have ransacked army and police arsenals in towns throughout the south in the past two weeks as protests over failed pyramid investment schemes turned into armed rebellion.
Tension rose further on Wednesday when civilians in Tirana seized weapons and trouble broke out in the northern city of Shkoder.
The rebels' key demand is the immediate resignation of President Sali Berisha and few of them appear keen to wait for early elections in June when a new parliament could vote to remove him.
